newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to seek charges in nuclear accident cover-up.
newsitem.headline: Japan to seek charges in nuclear accident cover-up.

text.p: The Japanese government will soon ask prosecutors to file charges against a state-run firm which has admitted a cover-up in its handling of the nation's worst nuclear accident, officials said on Tuesday.

The officials from the government's Science and Technology Agency said they would file a formal complaint with prosecutors or police as early as Wednesday against the state-run Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC).

The complaint, the first step in bringing formal charges against a person or institution, concerns a PNC cover-up of events leading up to an explosion at a nuclear reprocessing plant which exposed 37 workers to low levels of radiation.

Although none of the workers was seriously harmed, the March 11 explosion ranked as Japan's worst nuclear accident and intensified public concerns about the safety of the nation's big nuclear power programme.

Asked about the rare move by a government agency to initiate legal action against an affiliate, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters on Tuesday: "What do you mean by rare? It's rare enough to lie about things like this."

PNC officials admitted last week that a report into a fire and the subsequent explosion at the plant had been altered to state, falsely, that workers had checked to ensure that the blaze had been put out.

The report said staff made visual checks that the flames had been doused but in reality no such checks were made. The fire flared up again and triggered the explosion at a bituminisation facility inside the PNC's reprocessing complex in Tokaimura, 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo.
Low-level nuclear waste is mixed with asphalt at the facility to be placed in drums for permanent storage.
PNC officials also admitted there was a conspiracy to keep silent about the content of the false report.

Agency officials said the PNC may have violated a Japanese law governing the operation of nuclear reactors. Such an offence could carry a jail term of up to six months and a fine of 200,000 yen ($1,580).

"We have a grave interest in the case," said Deputy Chief Mito District Prosecutor Yuji Umemura, whose office would take charge of the case on receipt of a complaint. "If they are found to have violated the Nuclear Reactor Control Law, we will take strict measures."
The PNC would not comment on the case.

The cover-up has prompted opposition parties to prepare a no-confidence motion against Science and Technology Minister Riichiro Chikaoka, but Hashimoto has indicated his ruling party may kill the motion. Parliament is to consider the case next week.

Critics say the case has exposed a culture of secrecy at the PNC over mistakes, and many government officials have started calling for the break-up of the giant firm, which lies at the heart of Japan's ambitious nuclear power programme.
It is the second case of PNC deception over an accident at one of its nuclear facilities.

In December 1995, PNC officials admitted they had lied about inspections and tried to suppress videotape footage of a massive coolant leak at its experimental fast-breeder reactor, Monju. A PNC public relations official dealing with the Monju accident committed suicide after the cover-up was exposed. Although there was no radiation leak, Monju remains closed.

In the Monju case, however, the Science and Technology Agency did not file a complaint with prosecutors. Residents did so, but the case is still pending at the local district prosecutor's office. ($1=126 yen)
